Insipid

in-SIP-id · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insipid is boring, or lacking flavor or interest.

The soup was so insipid that the diners reached for the salt and pepper before taking a second bite.

Worked Example

Critics panned the sequel as insipid, a flat retread of the original with none of its wit or surprise.

Insipid applies just as easily to food, writing, or personality -- anything that fails to leave any real impression.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bland: mild or flavorless in a plain, neutral way; insipid is harsher, criticizing something as disappointingly dull and lifeless

dull: not interesting or exciting

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flavorful: having a strong, pleasant taste

zesty: full of lively flavor or energy

Where it sits · how empty of interest it is — plain → insipid → insipid

plain vs. insipid: A plain cracker isn't meant to be exciting.

insipid vs. insipid: An insipid book with no real ideas at all just isn't worth finishing.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root+suffix — sipid

root+suffix — sipid: tasty, flavorful (Latin (sapidus))

Put it together

Put it together: in- ("not") + sipid ("tasty") = lacking flavor or interest.

Use the root in a new word: sapient

Use the root in a new word: sapient: The deeper Latin root sapere ("to taste or to know") also survives in the rare word "sapient," meaning wise -- tasting and knowing share the same root in Latin.

Word Choice

Insipid works equally well for food that lacks flavor and for writing or people that lack any spark of interest.
